books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text:
Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), on the peoples of the United States:

“Three races naturally distinct, and I might almost say hostile to each other, are discoverable among them at the first glance. ... fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.”

“As soon as it is admitted that the whites and the emancipated blacks are placed upon the same territory in the situation of two alien communities, it will readily be understood that there are but two alternatives for the future; the negroes and the whites must either wholly part or wholly mingle.”

“I do not imagine that the white and black races will ever live in any country upon an equal footing.”

Background: Tocqueville, a French visitor, traveled in the United States in 1831–1832 and published Democracy in America in 1835.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (Reeve translation, 1835), public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (1835), public domain
stem: What did Tocqueville mean when he wrote that the three races 'do not amalgamate'?

options.text: They had never met before Tocqueville arrived
options.misconception: The passage says fortune brought them together on the same soil.

options.text: They shared the soil but stayed separate peoples
They had already blended into one American people
options.misconception: The passage says the opposite: they do not mix into one people.

options.text: They lived on separate continents and never traded
options.misconception: The passage places them together on the same soil.

rationales.A: The passage says fortune brought them together on the same soil. They had met; they had not mixed.
rationales.B: Mixed but not joined: the races shared the soil while each fulfilled its destiny apart.
rationales.C: Amalgamate means to blend into one. Tocqueville says plainly that they do not.
rationales.D: The passage puts all three on the same soil. Separate continents is the opposite of what he describes.
rationales.general:
1. Read the sentence slowly. The races are mixed on the same soil, yet they do not amalgamate.
2. Translate the hard word. To amalgamate is to blend into one people, so not amalgamating means staying apart.
3. Name the meaning. They shared the land while each race followed its own separate path.
Remember: when a writer says two things are mixed but not joined, look for the wall between them.
